[[Image:CanadianFleabaneEssentialOil.png|thumb|Canadian fleabane (''Erigeron canadensis'') essential oil in a clear glass vial]]

'''''Erigeron canadensis''''' ([[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] '''''Conyza canadensis''''') is an annual plant native throughout most of [[North America]] and [[Central America]]. It is also widely naturalized in [[Eurasia]] and [[Australia]]. Common names include '''horseweed''', '''Canadian horseweed''', '''Canadian fleabane''', '''coltstail''', '''marestail''', and '''butterweed'''. It was the first weed to have developed [[glyphosate]] resistance, reported in 2001 from [[Delaware]].

==Description==
''Erigeron canadensis'' is an [[annual plant|annual]], [[herbaceous plant]] growing to {{convert|1.5|m|ft|0|abbr=off}} tall, with sparsely hairy stems. The [[leaf|leaves]] are unstalked, slender, {{convert|2–10|cm|in|1|abbr=off}} long, and up to {{convert|1|cm|in|1|abbr=on}} wide, with a [[Leaf shape|coarsely toothed margin]]. They grow in an alternate spiral up the stem, and the lower ones wither early. The [[flower head]]s are produced in dense [[inflorescence]]s and are {{convert|1|cm|in|1|abbr=on}} in diameter. Each individual flower has a ring of white or pale purple [[ray florets]] and a centre of yellow [[disc floret]]s. The fruit is a [[cypsela (botany)|cypsela]] tipped with dirty white down.<ref name=NatureGate>{{cite web |url=http://www.luontoportti.com/suomi/en/kukkakasvit/canadian-fleabane |title=Canadian Fleabane: ''Conyza canadensis'' |publisher=NatureGate |access-date=2013-12-31}}</ref>

''Erigeron canadensis'' can easily be confused with ''[[Erigeron sumatrensis]]'', which may grow to a height of {{convert|2|m|ft|1|abbr=on}}, and the more hairy ''[[Erigeron bonariensis]]'', which does not exceed {{convert|1|m|ft|1|abbr=on}}. ''E. canadensis'' is distinguished by [[bract]]s that have a brownish inner surface with no red dot at the tip, and are free (or nearly free) of the hairs found on the bracts of the other species.<ref>[http://www.iewf.org/weedid/Conyza_sumatrensis.htm ''Conyza sumatrensis''], International Environmental Weed Foundation.</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.eattheweeds.com/conyza-canadensis-herb-fire-food-2 |title=Horseweed, Marestail  |first=Deane |last=Green |date=31 August 2011 |access-date=2014-08-09}}</ref><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200023708 Flora of North America, ''Conyza canadensis'' (Linnaeus) Cronquist, Bull. Torrey Bot. Club. 70: 632. 1943. Vergerette du Canada].</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Horseweed originated in [[North America]] and [[Central America]] and is widespread in its native range.<ref name=belanna>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Erigeron%20canadensis.png Biota of North America Program, 2014 county distribution map, ''Erigeron canadensis''].</ref> It has spread to inhabited areas of most of the temperate zone of Asia,<ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=242422265 Flora of China, ''Erigeron canadensis'' Linnaeus, Sp. Pl. 2: 863. 1753. <big>小蓬草</big> xiao peng cao ]</ref> Europe,<ref name=NatureGate/><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=erigeron+canadensis Altervista Flora Italiana, Cespica canadese, avoadinha, Berufkraut, ''Erigeron canadensis'' L.] includes photos and European distribution map</ref> and [[Australia]].<ref>[http://bie.ala.org.au/species/urn:lsid:biodiversity.org.au:apni.taxon:683151 Atlas of Living Australia, ''Conyza canadensis'' (L.) Cronquist Canadian Fleabane]</ref> It is found in [[Great Britain|Britain]] from northern [[Scotland]] to [[Cornwall]], growing as a weed of arable land and man-made environments. It is considered invasive in [[China]].<ref>{{Cite journal |doi=10.1111/1440-1703.12024 |title=Erigeron canadensis affects the taxonomic and functional diversity of plant communities in two climate zones in the North of China |year=2019 |last1=Wu |first1=Bingde |last2=Zhang |first2=Huanshi |last3=Jiang |first3=Kun |last4=Zhou |first4=Jiawei |last5=Wang |first5=Congyan |journal=Ecological Research |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=535–547 |bibcode=2019EcoR...34..535W |s2cid=198244222 }}</ref>

Horseweed can grow in a range of natural habitats, from [[sand dunes]] to old fields, as well as in gardens and other disturbed areas.<ref name= "Weakley">Weakley, A. S. (2015). Flora of the Southern and Mid-Atlantic States. Chapel Hill, NC, University of North Carolina Herbarium.</ref> It is an [[Ruderal species|indicator for disturbance]] because it often colonizes disturbed areas in which it was sparse or absent prior to the disturbance.<ref name= "Brewer">{{Cite journal |last1=Brewer |first1=J. Stephen |last2=Bertz |first2=Christine A. |last3=Cannon |first3=Jeffery B. |last4=Chesser |first4=Jason D. |last5=Maynard |first5=Erynn E. |date=March 2012 |title=Do natural disturbances or the forestry practices that follow them convert forests to early-successional communities? |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/225051161 |journal=Ecological Applications |volume=22 |issue=2 |pages=442–458 |doi=10.1890/11-0386.1 |issn=1051-0761 |jstor=41416774 |pmid=22611846 |bibcode=2012EcoAp..22..442B |access-date=19 July 2025}}</ref> Horseweed is a common pest of agricultural fields, and can tolerate a range of acidic to neutral soils (pH 4.8 to 7.2).<ref name= "guide">Tilley, D. 2012. Plant Guide for Canadian horseweed (''Conyza canadensis''). USDA-Natural Resources Conservation Service, Aberdeen, ID Plant Materials Center. 83210-0296.</ref>

==Weed status==
Horseweed is commonly considered a weed, and in [[Ohio]], [[Oregon]], and some other locations,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Appendix H.Noxious and Invasive WeedControlPlan |url=https://www.blm.gov/sites/blm.gov/files/documents/files/nv_rubypipeline_Appendix%20H%20Noxious%20Weed%20Plan.pdf}}</ref> it has been declared a [[noxious weed]].<ref>{{GRIN | access-date = 2017-12-18}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Noxious Weed Program {{!}} Deschutes County Oregon |url=https://www.deschutes.org/road/page/noxious-weed-program |access-date=2023-06-13 |website=www.deschutes.org}}</ref> It was the first weed to have developed [[glyphosate]] resistance, reported in 2001 from [[Delaware]].<ref name="Van Gessel">{{cite journal |last=VanGessel |first=Mark J. |year=2001 |title=Glyphosate-resistant horseweed from Delaware |journal=Weed Science |volume=49 |issue=6 |pages=703–705 |doi= 10.1614/0043-1745(2001)049[0703:RPRHFD]2.0.CO;2 |jstor=4046416 |s2cid=86256252 }}</ref>

It can be found in fields, meadows, and gardens throughout its native range. Horseweed infestations (specifically of 105 plants per 10 ft<sup>2</sup>) have reduced [[soybean]] yields by as much as 83%,<ref name="Weeds-2023">{{Cite web |title=Marestail (Horseweed) |url=https://www.canr.msu.edu/weeds/extension/marestail-horseweed |access-date=2023-06-13 |website=Weeds |language=en-us}}</ref> with one estimate claiming it can reduce yields by up to 90%.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Froemke |first=A. M. |date=April 24, 2020 |title=HORSEWEED (ERIGERON CANADENSIS) CONTROL IN NO-TILL SOYBEAN SYSTEMS ON A COARSE TEXTURED SOIL |url=https://library.ndsu.edu/ir/bitstream/handle/10365/31791/Horseweed%20(Erigeron%20canadensis)%20Control%20in%20No-Till%20Soybean%20Systems%20on%20a%20Coarse%20Textured%20Soil.pdf?sequence=1 |access-date=June 13, 2023 |website=North Dakota State University}}</ref> Severe infestations have reduced sugar beet yields by 64%.<ref name="Weeds-2023" />

It is an especially problematic weed in [[no-till agriculture]], as it is often resistant to [[glyphosate]]<ref name="Van Gessel" /> and other [[herbicides]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kruger |first1=Greg R. |last2=Davis |first2=Vince M. |last3=Weller |first3=Stephen C. |last4=Johnson |first4=William G. |year= 2010 |title=Growth and Seed Production of Horseweed ''(Conyza canadensis)'' Populations after Exposure to Postemergence 2,4-D. |journal=Weed Science |volume=58 |issue=4 |pages=413–419 |doi=10.1614/WS-D-10-00022.1|bibcode=2010WeedS..58..413K |s2cid=55366555 }}</ref> Farmers are advised to include [[2,4-D]] or [[dicamba]] in a burndown application prior to planting to control horseweed.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dilliott |first1=Meghan |last2=Soltani |first2=Nader |last3=Hooker |first3=David C. |last4=Robinson |first4=Darren E. |last5=Sikkema |first5=Peter H. |date=March 15, 2022 |title=When using glyphosate plus dicamba, 2,4-D, halauxifen or pyraflufen/2,4-D for glyphosate-resistant horseweed (Erigeron canadensis) control in soybean, which third mix partner is better, saflufenacil or metribuzin? |journal=Weed Technology |language=en |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=295–302 |doi=10.1017/wet.2022.18 |bibcode=2022WeedT..36..295D |issn=0890-037X|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Horseweed/Marestail |url=https://iwilltakeaction.com/weed/horseweed |access-date=2023-06-13 |website=Take Action |language=en |archive-date=2023-03-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230329153839/https://iwilltakeaction.com/weed/horseweed |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Ecology==
Horseweed produces a large amount of seeds that are dispersed by wind, allowing it to easily colonize disturbed soils.<ref name= "guide"/>

The seeds can germinate at any time of year with sufficient moisture and proper temperatures. With fall germination, it overwinters as a [[Rosette (botany)|rosette]] and bolts in the spring to flower in the summer. With spring germination, it spends less time as a rosette before bolting to flower.<ref name= "guide"/> The seeds can persist in the seedbank of disturbed and non-disturbed sites, though it is more prevalent in disturbed sites.<ref name= "Cohen">{{cite journal |last1=Cohen |first1=Susan |last2=Braham |first2=Richard |last3=Sanchez |first3=Felipe |title=Seed Bank Viability in Disturbed Longleaf Pine Sites |journal=Restoration Ecology |date=December 2004 |volume=12 |issue=4 |pages=503–515 |doi=10.1111/j.1061-2971.2004.00382.x |bibcode=2004ResEc..12..503C }}</ref>

The seeds are capable of persisting in the seedbank after a fire,<ref name= "Creech">Creech, M. N., et al. (2012). "Alteration and Recovery of Slash Pile Burn Sites in the Restoration of a Fire-Maintained Ecosystem." Restoration Ecology 20(4): 505-516.</ref> and the plant increases in frequency in response to more frequent fire regimes.<ref name= "Burton">Burton, J. A. (2009). Fire frequency effects on vegetation of an upland old growth forest in eastern Oklahoma. Environmental Science. Stillwater, Oklahoma, Oklahoma State University. Bachelor: 78.</ref>

''Erigeron canadensis'' is insect pollinated and is recorded to have been visited in northern Florida by ''[[Ceratina]]''.<ref>Ulyshen, M. D., K. Robertson, S. Horn, and C. Dixon. 2024. Characterization of the bee community and pollination network in a southeastern U.S. pine savanna. Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution 12:1403602.</ref>

==Uses==
The [[Zuni people]] insert the crushed flowers of ''E. canadensis'' var. ''canadensis'' into the [[nostrils]] to cause [[sneezing]], relieving [[rhinitis]].<ref>Stevenson, Matilda Coxe 1915 Ethnobotany of the Zuni Indians. SI-BAE Annual Report #30 (p.55).</ref> The [[Seminole people]] used it for cold and cough medicine, the [[Iroquois people]] used it to help combat fevers, and the [[Navajo]] and [[Chippewa]] peoples used it for stomach pain.<ref name= "guide"/> Other medicinal applications include use as a [[nervine]], [[stimulant]], and antiplasmodic (anti-parasitic specific to a genus of plasmids - malaria is one) .<ref>Rafinesque, C. S. (1828). Medical flora; or Manual of the medical botany of the United States of North America.</ref>
